item.description: arXiv:2610.15038v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.
item.dc:creator: Fan Pu, Keshu Wu, Jiwan Jiang, Shiyu Shen, Zhiwen Fan, Zhengzhong Tu, Jiachen Li, Yang Zhou

item.title: RELAGRAM: Recursive Latent Graph Model for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.15106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Latent recursion repeatedly processes internal representations through the same neural network. Recent work has shown this approach to be effective on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving. However, whether latent recursion can support neural routing remains unclear. We introduce RELAGRAM (Recursive Latent Graph Model), a novel approach that brings latent recursion to graph combinatorial optimization. RELAGRAM encodes a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) instance as edge tokens; a compact transformer recurrently updates the latent representations of these tokens. An output head maps the answer state to an edge heatmap, from which an autoregressive decoder constructs a feasible solution. On CVRP-100 instances, the 0.53M-parameter RELAGRAM achieves gaps to a PyVRP reference of 13.4%, 9.8%, and 8.3% under greedy decoding, eightfold symmetry augmentation, and 256-candidate search, respectively. Trained only on CVRP-100, RELAGRAM generalizes zero-shot to CVRP-500 and CVRP-1000, achieving gaps of 15.6% and 21.7% under 256-candidate search. Together, these results demonstrate that latent recursion is a promising approach to neural routing.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Kirill Bickov, Neil Yorke-Smith

item.title: An adaptive Galerkin neural-network method for minimum-norm control of wave equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.15220v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop an adaptive Galerkin neural-network method for computing minimum-$L^2$-norm interior controls for wave equations with spatially varying coefficients. Within the Hilbert Uniqueness Method, adjoint waves are approximated directly in space-time by least-squares Galerkin projections onto trial spaces enriched by neural-network basis functions selected through residual-based training. Linear Galerkin solves determine the adjoint approximations, and a separate linear system reconstructs the control. The least-squares objective provides an indicator for adaptive enrichment and stopping; the experiments use a Ritz-based terminal-data version whose continuous-error interpretation additionally requires an eigenpair consistency estimate. The main difficulty is that adjoint errors perturb this reconstruction system. Assuming observability of the continuous equation, we derive sufficient stability conditions involving a worst-case factor $\sqrt{n}$ multiplying the maximal adjoint error, where $n$ is the number of retained terminal modes. A fully discrete error estimate separates terminal-space truncation, adjoint approximation, and assembly errors, yielding convergence to the minimum-norm control when the truncation error, the $\sqrt{n}$-weighted adjoint error, and the assembly errors tend to zero as $n$ grows. For spectral terminal bases, additional regularity and uniform contraction assumptions yield quantitative convergence rates and show that $O(\log n)$ accepted enrichment steps per mode suffice to balance the neural and truncation errors. Numerical experiments on a nonconvex Cassini oval, a square containing a low-speed lens, and a three-dimensional ball with a graded coefficient illustrate the method.
item.dc:creator: Nguyen Gia Hien

item.title: Homogenization of an optimal control problem for a Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system in a 3D perforated domain
item.description: arXiv:2610.15584v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the homogenization of an optimal control problem governed by a Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system in a periodically perforated three-dimensional domain. The obstacles are Lipschitz sets of size $\varepsilon^\alpha$, $\alpha>3$, where $\varepsilon$ is the period. The fluid satisfies the no-slip condition on the outer boundary and the free-slip condition on the obstacles, the phase-field equation contains a source term, and the convective term carries a pore-scale Reynolds number that tends to zero as $\varepsilon\to0$. The control is a distributed body force, and the cost functional tracks the velocity in $L^2$ and the order parameter in $H^1$. Since uniqueness of weak solutions of the state system is not known for fixed $\varepsilon$, the control-to-state relation is multivalued, and we pose the microscopic problems over control-state pairs. We prove the existence of microscopic optimal pairs and the sequential $\Gamma$-convergence of the cost functionals to the cost functional of a control problem governed by the unsteady Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard system on the full domain. As a consequence, the optimal values converge, every cluster point of microscopic optimal pairs is optimal for the homogenized problem, and the optimal controls converge strongly along the corresponding subsequences. The $\liminf$ inequality follows from the homogenization of the state system, including the strong convergence of the gradients of the order parameter. Only the recovery sequence requires uniqueness of weak solutions of the homogenized system, which we prove when the outer boundary is of class $C^{2,1}$.
item.dc:creator: Amartya Chakrabortty, Haradhan Dutta, Hari Shankar Mahato

item.title: Quantum ordinal optimization under a fixed comparison budget
item.description: arXiv:2610.15791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ordinal optimization selects designs that are good enough rather than optimal when evaluation is expensive and the budget is small. The alignment probability measures the chance that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good designs. We formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize this probability under a fixed oracle budget. We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that a knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the optimum. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design's rank has a polynomial probability law. At the same comparison budget, the maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, a factor attained whenever there are more than twice as many designs as comparisons, so a quantum algorithm can realize rank laws that no classical algorithm with the same budget can. We determine the exact quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set. For selecting the best of n designs, the optimal success probability with one quantum comparison is approximately 3.30/n for large n, compared with 2/n for one classical comparison. When the best design is sought, one quantum comparison gives a higher alignment probability than two classical comparisons whenever there are more than nine designs.
item.dc:creator: Hongyu Wu

item.title: The $p$-Bures-Wasserstein distance via $3\times3$ block matrices (with application to $p$-Bures-Wasserstein barycenters)
item.description: arXiv:2610.15889v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the $p$-Bures-Wasserstein distance $D_p(A,B)=(\mathrm{tr}\,A^p+\mathrm{tr}\,B^p-2\|A^{1/2}B^{1/2}\|_p^p)^{1/2}$ on positive semidefinite matrices; it equals the Bures-Wasserstein distance for $p=1$, and the Hilbert-Schmidt distance for $p=2$. We prove that $D_p$ is a metric for every $1\le p\le2$, by proving a stronger 2014 conjecture of Lin and van den Driessche on $3\times3$ block matrices. Our main tool is a partition inequality for Schatten norms, proved by complex interpolation. We also characterize Fr\'echet means for $D_p$ by a fixed-point equation and prove geometric convergence of the associated iteration.
item.dc:creator: Suvrit Sra

item.title: Two Linear Programs are Better than One
item.description: arXiv:2610.15909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity. First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrube\v{s} that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.
item.dc:creator: Alexander E. Black, Christoph Hertrich, Stefan Kober, Georg Loho

item.title: A Mean Field Model of Consumption Inertia and Keeping Up with the Joneses
item.description: arXiv:2610.16019v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Households compare their living standard with others' and dislike changing it. We study consumption and investment when felicity depends on consumption relative to a benchmark, the population's geometric average consumption, and cuts in felicity weigh more than increases. Asset returns are exogenous. For finitely many types and arbitrary initial wealth and inherited standards, a mean field equilibrium exists under a weak interaction condition, and for fixed budget multipliers the benchmark is the fixed point of a contraction. In a complete market with common risk, a mean field equilibrium at empirical type frequencies is an exact Nash equilibrium of the finite game, for any preferences over relative consumption. We bound the gain from deviating when plans computed at another composition are used. We compute equilibria in which groups with different wealth, inherited standards, and loss aversion revise spending at different dates. With identical households and common risk, the unique symmetric equilibrium is the policy of a single loss averse household with modified curvature. In a baseline example, ignoring the inherited standard costs up to 17% of wealth, while small errors about the composition of the reference group cost less than 0.5%.
item.dc:creator: Junkee Jeon

item.title: Online Submodular Welfare Maximization: Computation is not the Bottleneck
item.description: arXiv:2610.16060v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We revisit the online submodular welfare maximization problem (OSW), a vast generalization of numerous well-studied online allocation problems, including online bipartite matching, display ads and AdWords. A natural greedy OSW algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of $1/2$ [LLN06], and $1-1/e$ under i.i.d. arrivals [KPV13]. Both bounds are tight for polynomial-time algorithms unless NP=RP [KPV13]. The information-theoretic limits for OSW, in contrast, remained open. This prompted researchers to ask for tighter upper bounds [Mehta13] or conjecture the existence of better-competitive (slow) algorithms [Huang23, LTX+23, CHS24, Huang2024, HTW24}. We resolve Mehta's question and refute the subsequent conjectures, proving that the greedy algorithm is in fact tight for both adversarial and i.i.d. arrivals, regardless of computation time. Seemingly contradicting recent $(1-1/e)$-competitive fractional algorithms for OSW [HJP+24,Patton26], we show that this impossibility even holds for fractional algorithms, provided their outputs correspond to marginals that are roundable in hindsight. Conceptually, our proofs can be seen as identifying that a bottleneck for OSW, even under (deterministic) adversarial arrivals, is the inherently random notion of correlation gap [ADSY12].
item.dc:creator: Rajan Udwani, David Wajc

item.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2610.16187v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.
item.dc:creator: Hwanwoo Kim, Jungwoo Hong, Kyungjae Lee

item.title: Optimal Synthesis on the Special Linear Group
item.description: arXiv:2610.16222v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the exponential map on the group of real two-by-two matrices with determinant one, endowed with a left-invariant Riemannian metric. Using the Euler-Poincar\'e equation and its linearization, we determine the conjugate and Maxwell times and identify a domain on which the exponential map is a global diffeomorphism onto the complement of the Maxwell stratum. This provides an alternative proof that the first Maxwell time coincides with the cut time. We obtain an explicit matrix description of the cut locus and characterize the globally minimizing geodesics. Furthermore, we analyze the first Maxwell-time function, determine its unique global minimum, and show that the injectivity radius is $\frac{\pi \sqrt{14}}{4}$. Finally, we characterize the intersection of the cut and conjugate loci and prove that every geodesic is equi-optimal.
item.dc:creator: Marcus T. C. Lau, Alejandro Bravo-Doddoli

item.title: Some remarks on nonexistence in the Gamow liquid drop model
item.description: arXiv:2610.16306v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper we deal with the celebrated Gamow liquid drop model, namely, for $m>0$, $N\geq 2$ and $\alpha\in (0,N)$, we study the problem \[ \min\Big\{P(\Omega)+ V_\alpha(\Omega) : \Omega\subset \mathbb{R}^N,\;|\Omega|=m\Big\}\,, \] and focus mostly on the nonexistence of minimizers for large masses. First we show that any possible minimizer in the asymptotic regime must satisfy an optimal thickness property. Eventually, in the simplified setting of sets made up as a tiling of cubes, we show that nonexistence occurs for large masses for the whole range of parameters $N\geq 2$ and $\alpha\in (0,N)$.
item.dc:creator: Dario Mazzoleni, Aldo Pratelli, Berardo Ruffini

item.title: Equilibria and consensus in discrete-time opinion dynamics with mixed weighted-averaging and weighted-median mechanisms
item.description: arXiv:2610.16406v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Opinion dynamics models relate interpersonal influence to consensus or persistent disagreement. We study a discrete-time model combining weighted-average and weighted-median updates on a fixed directed network. Individuals update synchronously with possibly different adjustment coefficients. We characterize equilibria through local balance conditions and opinion level sets, and establish convergence to a Lyapunov-stable equilibrium using nonexpansiveness and Krasnosel'skii--Mann theory. We define type-dependent cohesive sets: each weighted-average member assigns all its weight to the set, whereas each weighted-median member assigns at least one half. Consensus is reached from every initial condition if and only if no two such sets are disjoint. Otherwise, an open set of initial conditions leads to persistent disagreement. Replacing weighted-median individuals by weighted-average individuals preserves consensus whenever it is already guaranteed for all initial conditions. Four numerical studies examine the number and locations of weighted-average individuals. The frequency of reaching a prescribed consensus tolerance is nondecreasing with their fraction in the sampled ensembles, but individual realizations need not follow this trend.
item.dc:creator: Junkai Cheng, Wenjun Mei

item.title: Asymptotic Risk of Learning-Rate Schedules for Least-Squares Regression with Discretely Distributed Features
item.description: arXiv:2610.16518v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on streaming least squares with discretely distributed features (Slock's model), which decouples the dynamics across eigendirections. Under power-law source and capacity conditions, we derive the exact finite-time risk and asymptotic equivalents of constant and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedules. With a tuned base learning-rate, the resulting scaling law decays as $\Theta(T^{-q})$, where $T$ is the horizon, and $q$ is independent of the cooldown length $c \in (0,1]$ but is strictly smaller for the constant schedule: any cooldown of fixed relative length $c > 0$, however short, improves the risk by a polynomial factor, while its length only affects the constant, which is minimized by linear decay ($c = 1$). Finally, we show that the optimal risk depends on the batch size $b$ and horizon $T$ only through $bT$, up to a critical batch size.
item.dc:creator: No\'e Colomban, Francis Bach, Fabian Schaipp

item.title: Scalable Identification of Physics-Based and Neural Dynamics from Partial Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2610.16559v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a scalable method for identifying nonlinear dynamics from partial measurements, supporting physics-based, neural-network, and gray-box models. We use the Prediction Error Method (PEM) coupled with state estimation performed by a Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) scheme, which can account directly for general nonlinear dynamics. This results in a bi-level optimization problem that scales poorly with increasing model parameters. To improve computational efficiency, we derive a reformulation that avoids explicit parameter-wide sensitivity matrices and exploits the temporal structure of the underlying optimization problem. Numerical comparisons show up to a $215\times$ speedup in hypergradient evaluation. Racing-vehicle simulations demonstrate accurate prediction and physical-parameter recovery in tire-force identification. Real-world data show that the gray-box model improves prediction accuracy with a neural residual while retaining physical interpretability.
item.dc:creator: Yibo Zhou, Johannes K\"ohler

item.title: Minimal time for heat observability on almost-Riemannian surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.16568v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We determine the minimal observation time for the heat equation on a closed almost-Riemannian surface, for a class of observation sets leaving sufficiently thin collars around simple Baouendi-Grushin circles. The structure and density are analytic near these circles, and the coefficients may depend on both variables. The formula is expressed through a complex phase describing concentration near the singular set and extends the thresholds known for separated models. Regular unobserved regions away from the circles do not change this time, provided all other singularities are observed. For singular circles of constant bracket step greater than two, local analyticity implies failure of observability at every time for observation sets at positive distance. We also construct quasimodes concentrated near simple singular circles, with exponentially small errors. Their superpositions give a lower bound for the Schr\"odinger observation time.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Boulard, Amaury Hayat, Emmanuel Tr\'elat

item.title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
item.description: arXiv:2610.16716v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer simulations provide detailed predictions for microchannel heat sinks but can be computationally demanding when many geometries and operating conditions are evaluated. This study develops a versatile two-layer model (VTLM) that reduces the three-dimensional problem to two coupled two-dimensional fields while retaining the in-plane geometry of the flow passages and fins. Effects associated with the unresolved channel-height direction are incorporated through hydraulic and thermal closures that account for wall friction and the fluid- and fin-side contributions to interlayer heat transfer. The closures are evaluated from the representative channel geometry, flow-development condition, and fin configuration. The VTLM was assessed against three-dimensional reference models across broad ranges of channel aspect ratios and operating conditions, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements. Compared with the existing two-layer models, the VTLM showed improved overall agreement with the three-dimensional reference results. The results showed that prediction accuracy was governed mainly by the flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, from which a conservative screening guideline was proposed for the examined straight-channel configurations. The assessment of finned expansion--contraction channels further supported the applicability of the VTLM to the investigated passages with abrupt width changes. Overall, the VTLM provides a reduced-dimensional framework for thermohydraulic analysis across the range of microchannel heat-sink configurations examined in this study without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.
item.dc:creator: Chih-Hsiang Chen, Kentaro Yaji

item.title: A Deterministic $0.401$-Approximation for Non-monotone Submodular Maximization under Matroid Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.16785v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Submodular maximization arises in a wide range of combinatorial optimization problems and has been extensively studied from the perspective of approximation algorithms. For maximizing nonnegative, non-monotone submodular functions subject to a matroid constraint, randomized algorithms achieve a $0.401$-approximation, whereas obtaining comparable deterministic guarantees remains challenging. In this paper, we present a deterministic $0.401$-approximation algorithm in the exact value and independence oracle model, improving upon the previous deterministic guarantee of $(0.385-\varepsilon)$ \cite{ChenGLSZ2026}. Our algorithm builds on the extended multilinear extension and provides a deterministic implementation of the recursive guided framework underlying the randomized $0.401$-approximation algorithm. The main technical ingredient is a direction oracle supported on at most two partitioned matroid bases. This oracle simultaneously satisfies the growth condition required by the extended-multilinear update and an approximate stationarity condition needed to construct the recursive guides. The resulting finite-support representation enables exact evaluation of the relevant expectations and marginal values without random sampling. The algorithm uses polynomially many value- and independence-oracle queries.
item.dc:creator: Shengminjie Chen, Kaifeng Lin, Xiaoming Sun, Jialin Zhang

item.title: Venusian Radio Occultation Constellation Design and Reconfiguration Problems: A Benders Decomposition Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.16807v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Driven by the scientific value of Venusian atmospheric studies, numerous missions, such as Magellan and Venus Express, have relied on single-spacecraft radio occultation (RO) experiments. Despite their proven success, data throughput is inherently limited by the use of a single transmitter and its relative geometry with respect to Earth-based receivers. Therefore, the literature proposes leveraging a constellation of spacecraft to increase RO measurement opportunities and improve spatial and temporal coverage; however, current efforts impose strict simplifying assumptions that limit their applicability and responsiveness to complex mission narratives. Beyond initial constellation design, evolving mission objectives may require event-based constellation reconfiguration during operations. To address both design and operational needs, we propose two problems formulated as integer linear programs: the RO Constellation Configuration Design Problem and the RO Constellation Reconfiguration Problem. Further, we address the programs' solution-space explosion with a Benders decomposition approach. Numerical experiments show the applicability of our problems for constellation configuration design, tackle the full mission pipeline, transitioning from global atmospheric profiling to on-demand regional profiling above areas of volcanic interest, and show that the Benders decomposition approach efficiently obtains high-quality solutions to large-scale instances.
item.dc:creator: David O. Williams Rogers, Trupti P. Gosavi, Hang Woon Lee

item.title: Feature Normalization under Finite Training Budgets
item.description: arXiv:2610.16845v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standardizing a rare feature can help stochastic gradient descent learn its effect within a finite budget, but it also changes the noise cost of learning. We characterize the lowest rare-subgroup risks attainable by standardized and unscaled training when each chooses a nonnegative constant learning rate and a deterministic stopping time under the same observation cap. For two independent binary features, we derive both optimized risks as prevalence vanishes while the expected number of rare observations remains finite. Uniform control over rates and stopping times reduces each limiting oracle to a scalar minimization. With positive noise, the preferred scaling changes exactly once as we move signal to the rare feature while the limiting risk at initialization stays fixed and positive. The formulas also explain how noise and budget affect the comparison. Separate finite-prevalence bounds favor standardization on a rare-dominant signal family and unscaled training on a common-dominant family. The results concern final iterates with population preprocessing and fresh observations. Exact-moment searches assess the approximation at finite prevalence. In a controlled study, both orderings persist under observation reuse, estimated preprocessing, and intercept fitting when tuning choices are fixed before evaluation. Selecting a predictor after observing training can reverse an ordering, even when selection uses exact population risk.
item.dc:creator: Johan Larsson

item.title: GpFlash: Maximizing Speed and Minimizing Memory for Gaussian Process Training and Prediction
item.description:
arXiv:2610.16861v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents GpFlash, a Gaussian process library that is focused on fast training and posterior evaluations, minimal memory usage, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. GpFlash was compared to the popular GP libraries scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT on a MacBook Pro and the supercomputer Trillium. GpFlash was found to use less memory and to be faster for training and posterior evaluations relative to the other GP libraries for all cases considered. For example, when using $
x = 10^4$ training points in a 10-dimensional space GpFlash required 9.6 to 35 times less memory and was 2.6 to 54 times faster than the other GP libraries for the evaluation of the marginal log likelihood and its gradient. The memory reduction was achieved by only using one matrix of size $
x 	imes 
x$ to store different symmetric matrices in its lower and upper triangular entries. The computational speedup was the result of designing algorithms to access memory efficiently, using BLAS and LAPACK methods extensively, and factoring kernel equations so that expensive exponential calculations could be reused. GpFlash was more than 440 times faster than all of the other GP libraries considered when evaluating the posterior mean together with its gradient for the case with $10^4$ training points and 10 dimensions. GpFlash is available at https://github.com/marchildon/gpflash.
item.dc:creator: Andre Marchildon

item.title: Edge-preserving Bayesian neural networks via hierarchical sparsity-promoting priors
item.description: arXiv:2610.17023v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recovering piecewise-smooth functions with jump discontinuities from noisy, indirect, and incomplete data is a central task in computational inverse problems. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) with heavy-tailed weight priors have emerged as effective edge-preserving priors for such problems. However, posterior inference for these models remains computationally challenging, and existing approaches settle for point estimates obtained by directly optimizing heavy-tailed log-densities. We propose GSBL-BNNs, which model the neural network parameters hierarchically using sparsity-promoting priors from generalized sparse Bayesian learning (GSBL). The hierarchical formulation recovers several popular marginal priors, including Laplace and Student's $t$ (including Cauchy). A key modeling ingredient, novel among edge-preserving BNNs and native to the hierarchical formulation, couples each neuron's bias to its weights through a shared hyperparameter, so that the induced jump discontinuities are free to occur anywhere in the domain while the conditionally Gaussian structure underlying efficient inference is preserved. Furthermore, we develop a block-coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm for maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation. This BCD approach alternates between standard network training with iteratively reweighted $\ell^2$-regularization and exact, closed-form hyperparameter updates for gamma and inverse gamma hyperpriors. Building on the BCD algorithm, we perform approximate Bayesian inference and uncertainty quantification (UQ) using deep ensembles. Computational experiments---including signal denoising, deblurring, and inverting a two-dimensional hyperbolic conservation law--- show that GSBL-BNNs deliver accurate, edge-preserving reconstructions with built-in UQ. Compared with Gaussian- and Cauchy-BNNs, they yield more accurate predictive means and avoid overconfident uncertainty estimates.
item.dc:creator: Jan Habscheid, Jan Glaubitz

item.title: A Controlled Null Result for Per-Gate Riemannian Optimization in VQE
item.description: arXiv:2610.17395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parametrized gates in a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) live on a product of unitary groups, which makes Riemannian optimization a natural candidate for improving training. We test this candidate in the clean per-gate setting: each single-qubit gate is optimized directly on U (2) and compared with Adam on an unconstrained Euler-angle chart representing the same physical gate, initialized from the same unitaries and tuned with a separate learning-rate sweep. On a validated hydrogen-chain benchmark, we find no measurable practical advantage from the Riemannian machinery. The direct manifold optimizer and the Euler-coordinate baseline are interleaved in final error and success rate; the classical coordinate baseline is not slower in iterations on the successful cells; and the choices of Riemannian metric, retraction, and momentum vector transport do not change the conclusion. We also identify four failure modes that can manufacture an apparent positive result: a trivial product-state benchmark, a projected-matrix Adam baseline that discards most of its own step, a non-unitary inherited Cayley retraction that lets the reported energy pass below the variational minimum, and a learning-rate grid whose optimum sits at its boundary. Each failure mode produced a plausible multi-seed result in our own workflow before being caught. The practical output of this paper is therefore a controlled null result and a validation checklist for VQE optimizer comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Polina Belozerova, Pavel Osinenko

item.title: Risk-Averse Inference-Time Diffusion Model Alignment with Finite-Sample Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2610.17579v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Inference-time alignment steers diffusion models toward downstream objectives without costly fine-tuning, but existing methods typically optimize expected cost (or reward) without explicitly controlling tail risk. In this work, we propose a risk-averse framework for inference-time alignment of diffusion models that balances expected cost and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) under trajectory-level Kullback-Leibler regularization. We characterize the optimal path distribution and reverse transitions as functions of the CVaR threshold, reducing the alignment problem to a one-dimensional optimization problem over the threshold. We show that this one-dimensional optimization problem can be nonconvex in general, establish sufficient conditions for convexity, and introduce quadratic regularization to enable efficient derivative-free ternary search. Under suitable assumptions, we provide finite-sample guarantees for threshold optimization and value estimation, and combine them into a terminal total-variation bound relative to the regularized target under exact resampling. Experiments on synthetic data and image generation using Stable Diffusion demonstrate improved tail performance over risk-neutral baselines while maintaining competitive average cost.
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Liang, Xian Yu

item.title: Stability Transfer for Autonomous Systems via Higher-Order Taylor-Truncated Lyapunov Certificates
item.description: arXiv:2610.17604v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop analytical sufficient conditions for certifying the local asymptotic stability of nonlinear autonomous systems based on Lyapunov functions derived from their finite-order Taylor polynomial approximations. This approach translates the stability analysis problem from the original nonlinear dynamics to a more computationally tractable polynomial domain. The derived conditions allow for the explicit calculation of a guaranteed inner approximation of the region of attraction ($\mathrm{ROA}$). We show how sum-of-squares (SOS) programming and grid search can be used to systematically search for polynomial Lyapunov functions that yield a large certified threshold radius and extract a certified invariant set inner approximation of the $\mathrm{ROA}$ of the nonpolynomial original system. The framework is then applied to a control tuning problem: finding reduced-effort Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) controllers that ensure that a given initial state of interest belongs to the certified $\mathrm{ROA}$ of the nonpolynomial closed loop system. The effectiveness of the overall methodology is demonstrated using a pendulum with nonlinear damping and a nonlinear control system.
item.dc:creator: Jose D. Hoyos, Zehui Lu, Shaoshuai Mou

item.title: Inclusion-wise extremal knapsack problems are (mostly) hard to approximate
item.description: arXiv:2610.18017v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study two inclusion-wise extremal variants of the 0-1 Knapsack Problem (KP). Given $n$ items with integer weights and nonnegative costs or profits, the Minimum-Cost Maximal Knapsack Packing Problem seeks a minimum-cost packing for capacity $c$ to which no item can be added, while the Maximum-Profit Minimal Knapsack Cover Problem seeks a maximum-profit cover for threshold $d$ from which no item can be removed. Both problems are weakly $\mathrm{NP}$-hard and pseudo-polynomially solvable, as is the classical KP, but their approximability is fundamentally different: unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, with positive values neither problem admits a polynomial-time $2^{p(n)}$-approximation for any polynomial $p$; allowing zero values rules out every multiplicative factor. Even with unit costs for packing and unit profits for covering, neither admits an $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, whereas a trivial $n$-approximation exists. We identify restrictions that restore approximability. If every item weighs at least a fixed fraction of the capacity, respectively of the threshold, both problems can be solved exactly in polynomial time. For the cover problem, if each weight $w_i$ satisfies $w_i-1\ge\delta(d-1)$, we give an approximation scheme for arbitrary profits whose running time is polynomial in $n$, $1/\varepsilon$, and $1/\delta$. If values equal weights, a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) was already known for the packing problem; we give an FPTAS for the cover problem, improving on the previously known factor $2$. If value-to-weight ratios differ by at most a factor $\kappa$, we obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)\kappa$-approximation for both problems.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Ciccarelli, Fabio Furini, Ulrich Pferschy, Elena Rener

item.title: How to Train Your Intercept: A Comparison of Intercept Update Strategies in Coordinate Descent
item.description: arXiv:2610.18043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coordinate descent solvers for regularized generalized linear models (GLMs) differ in how they update the intercept. This seemingly routine choice can substantially affect convergence when the response is imbalanced. For direct coordinate descent on the original GLM loss, we compare a conservative step based on worst-case curvature, a safeguarded Newton step based on current curvature, and repeated Newton steps that solve the intercept subproblem. The conservative update can leave much of the interaction between the intercept and the coefficients unresolved, producing a slowdown when that interaction controls convergence. A single Newton step avoids this attenuation and, in our experiments, follows nearly the same outer trajectory as exact minimization while requiring fewer inner steps. Simulated and real-data experiments, including comparisons across six production solvers and a controlled intervention within skglm, support this explanation. We also show how the same mechanism appears in quadratic-approximation methods and extends to multinomial models with rare classes. We recommend a safeguarded Newton update for direct coordinate descent and full intercept optimization within frozen local quadratic surrogates.
item.dc:creator: Johan Larsson, Frederik Fabricius-Bjerre

item.title: Hyperelastic Modeling of Cardiac Tissue Deformation for Data Registration
item.description: arXiv:2610.18207v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work proposes a biomechanical registration framework designed to combine functional optical-mapping data with structural high-resolution MRI of cardiac tissue. The two acquisitions are performed in different mechanical configurations: optical mapping is obtained after stretching the sample, whereas MRI is acquired in a fixed resting state. To estimate the deformation between these configurations, the tissue is modeled as a nearly incompressible transversely isotropic hyperelastic material, and the traction amplitude is identified from optical-map marker positions through an inverse problem. Two-and threedimensional simulations show physically admissible deformations and provide a first proof of concept for the proposed strategy.

item.title: Generic Local Identifiability Does Not Imply Generic Global Identifiability in Linear Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.18228v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a counterexample to the implication from generic local to generic global identifiability for linear networks with a fixed topology, independently unknown edge coefficients, and selected excited and measured nodes. A six-node network with nine unknown coefficients has exactly two compatible parameter vectors generically. Adding six excited and measured nodes preserves this ambiguity while making the added coefficients directly recoverable. The resulting twelve-node structure has forty-two independent unknown coefficients and zero diagonal. For every positive bound on the largest eigenvalue magnitude, a nonempty open set of parameters has two distinct compatible networks satisfying that bound. This holds for both real and complex coefficients. Other open regions have exactly one admissible solution. The proof uses a rational transformation exchanging the two solutions and a common limiting matrix whose fourth power vanishes. Exact rational-number certificates verify an explicit pair. The construction also extends algebraically when the unknown coordinates are whole rational transfer functions. Genericity in prescribed numerator and denominator coefficient families, and the requirement that every transfer function vanish at infinite frequency, remain separate questions.
item.dc:creator: Anders Hansson

item.title: On Over-Conservatism Under Low-Probability Extreme Events: A KL-Regularized Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Planning Method
item.description: arXiv:2610.18290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy makes power systems more vulnerable to low-probability extreme events, elevating system planning to a critical role in ensuring reliability. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) based on the Wasserstein distance is widely used to address this challenge. However, we find that the conventional Wasserstein ambiguity set tends to excessively amplify the probabilities of low-probability extreme events, leading to over-conservative investment decisions. To mitigate this over-conservatism, this paper proposes a novel ambiguity set that modifies the Wasserstein distance with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence regularization term. By leveraging the KL divergence's sensitivity to relative probability changes, the proposed set effectively curbs the unrealistic magnification of low-probability events. A two-stage distributionally robust planning model built upon this new ambiguity set is developed to optimize the installed capacity of photovoltaic, wind, and energy storage. The complex model is then reformulated as an equivalent exponential cone program with strict theoretical proofs, making it computationally tractable. Numerical results on the PJM 5-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems reveal the over-conservatism of standard Wasserstein DRO under low-probability extreme events and validate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed planning model and solution algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Xinda Shen, Yifan Su, Bo Hu, Yanbo Chen, Changzheng Shao, Tao Wu

item.title: A Practical Combinatorial Interior Point Method for Minimum-Cost Flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.18328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In a recent breakthrough, Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg, and Sachdeva (arXiv:2203.00671) designed the first almost-linear-time algorithm for minimum-cost flow. Their approach uses an Interior Point Method (IPM) to achieve complexity $m^{1+o(1)}\log U \log C$. However, the $m^{1+o(1)}$ factor hides intricate recursive data structures, large constants and multiple log factors. In this paper, we give an implementation following the core ideas of their IPM with practical data structures and empirically obtained decision rules. We compare our solver with the cost scaling and network simplex solvers of LEMON on the instance families of the DIMACS Flow Challenge 2.0 core benchmark. Our implementation scales competitively on five of twelve families and better on two. On grid_wide we observe close to linear scaling: $m^{1.04}$ against $m^{1.48}$ for LEMON. We read these results as first evidence that the almost-linear-time framework can be relevant in practice, discuss our insights gained during the implementation process, and motivate where future work should focus to bridge the theory-practice gap.
item.dc:creator: Emil Sch\"atzle, Simon Meierhans, Rasmus Kyng, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg

item.title: Viscosity Solutions for Hamilton-Jacobi equations on Separable Banach Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.18496v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work provides a framework to treat optimal control problems on separable Banach spaces in the viscosity sense. First, it extends the notion of $B$-viscosity solutions to the Banach setting and relates the extension to the notions of viscosity solutions used in metric space settings. As the main results, the paper proves a strict comparison principle and characterizes the value function of an optimal control problem as the unique viscosity solution to an infinite-dimensional HJB equation.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Fuchs

item.title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped SGD with Linear Decay
item.description: arXiv:2610.18555v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we study the last-iterate convergence of clipped stochastic gradient descent under heavy-tailed noise. We assume that the stochastic gradients are unbiased and that the noise has a bounded central $p$-th moment, where $1<p\le2$. For smooth convex objectives, a linearly decreasing learning rate gives a high-probability error bound of order $O(LR^2\log(1/\delta)/T+\sigma R(\log(1/\delta)/T)^{(p-1)/p})$. We further establish last-iterate guarantees for nonsmooth composite objectives and smooth composite objectives with proximal updates. In addition, when a causal adversary replaces at most $q$ gradients, the same clipped update achieves a bound with $\log(1/\delta)$ replaced by $\log(1/\delta)+q$. The corresponding lower bounds for the clean and corrupted oracle models are also provided.
item.dc:creator: Wei Jiang, Haomin Bai, Zechao Li

item.title: Orientation Estimation of Cryo-EM Images for Molecules with Arbitrary Symmetry by Semidefinite Programming
item.dc:creator: Yunpeng Shi, Amit Singer, Jinxin Wang, Ruiyi Yang

item.title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
item.description: arXiv:2610.18739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.
item.dc:creator: Neil Walton

item.title: Optimality conditions with cone-generalized convex vector functions
item.description: arXiv:1408.5458v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The object of investigation in this paper are generalized convex vector nonlinear programming problems with cone constraints. We prove that a quasiconvex vector function is pseudoconvex with respect to the same cone if and only if every vector critical point of the function is a weak global minimizer, a result, which is a natural extension of a known characterization of pseudoconvex scalar functions. We introduce a new notion of a Fr\'echet differentiable pseudoconvex problem. We derive that a problem with quasiconvex vector data is pseudoconvex if and only if every Fritz John vector critical point is a weakly efficient global solution. Thus, we generalize a lot of previous optimality conditions, concerning the scalar case and the multiobjective Paretian one. We also introduce the notion of a Fritz John cone-pseudoinvex vector problem. We prove that a problem with cone constraints is Fritz John pseudoinvex if and only if every vector critical point of Fritz John type is a weak global minimizer with respect to the considered cone..
item.dc:creator: Vsevolod I. Ivanov

item.title: On the existence of infinitely many realization functions of non-global local minima for artificial neural networks with ReLU activation
item.description: arXiv:2202.11481v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gradient descent (GD) type optimization schemes are standard tools for training fully connected feedforward artificial neural networks (ANNs) with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation and can be considered as temporal discretizations of solutions of gradient flow (GF) differential equations. It is known that, for shallow ReLU ANNs, the risk of every bounded GF trajectory converges under suitable assumptions to the risk of a critical point, a zero of the corresponding gradient function. This motivates studying necessary and sufficient conditions in GF and GD convergence analysis for critical points and their dependence on problem parameters, such as the target function. In the first main result, we prove for shallow ReLU ANNs that for every dimension $d \in \mathbb{N}$, every $a \in \mathbb{R}$, $b \in (a, \infty)$, and every positive $\delta \in (0, \infty)$, there exists a Lipschitz continuous target function $f \colon [a, b]^d \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, for every hidden-layer width $\mathfrak{h} \in \mathbb{N} \cap (1, \infty)$, there are uncountably many different realization functions of non-global local minimum points whose risks exceed the infimum of the risk function by more than $\delta$. In the second main result, we show that, for shallow ReLU ANNs with only one neuron on each layer and a continuous piecewise polynomial target function, there exist at most finitely many different realization functions of critical points.
item.dc:creator: Shokhrukh Ibragimov, Arnulf Jentzen, Timo Kr\"oger, Adrian Riekert

item.title: Optimal and Self Selection of Service Type in a Queueing System where Long Service Postpones the Need for the Next Service
item.description: arXiv:2208.09348v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a make-to-order system with a finite set of customers. Production is stochastic with a nonlinear dependence between the ordered quantity and the production rate. Customers may have to queue until their turn arrives, and therefore their order decisions interact. Specifically, while being served, customers are aware of the queue length and choose one of two order quantities (or service types). The time to the next replenishment (their activity time) is stochastic and depends on the order quantities. A customer is inactive during service and while waiting in the queue. We refer to the type of service with a greater ratio of expected activity to service time as ``more efficient''. In the centralized case, the system is interested in maximizing the steady-state average number of active customers, which is referred to as the efficiency of the system. We show that choosing the more efficient service is not always optimal, but the optimal strategy can be approximated well by selecting one of three threshold strategies which depend on the number of inactive customers. In the decentralized case, each customer acts to maximize the fraction of time she is active. We observe that individuals and the manager have opposite incentives: When the queue is long, individuals tend to choose the long service, while the manager prefers the short service in this case. This makes the system difficult to regulate. However, we show that simply removing the less efficient service significantly increases efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Refael Hassin, Jiesen Wang

item.title: Projecting onto a Capped Rotated Second-Order Cone
item.description: arXiv:2307.07290v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We derive a closed-form expression for the projection onto a capped rotated second-order cone, a convex set that arises in perspective relaxations of nonlinear programs with binary indicator variables. The closed-form solution involves four distinct cases, one of which coincides with the classical projection onto a secondorder cone. The remaining three cases involve a nontrivial analysis in determining the necessary and sufficient conditions under which the solution lies on the intersection of the cone and a facet of a box. Beyond theoretical interest, this result enables the development of efficient projection-based first-order methods for optimization problems involving perspective reformulations. As an illustration, we consider the continuous perspective relaxation of sparse logistic regression, whose feasible region contains a Cartesian product of capped rotated second-order cones. Computational experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate that accelerated projected-gradient, together with computing our closed-form projection at each iteration, improves on the running time of a general first-order conic solver while obtaining solutions of similar accuracy. These results highlight the practical value of the proposed projection formula for solving continuous relaxations of perspective formulations of mixed-integer second-order cone problems.
item.dc:creator: Noam Goldberg, Ishy Zagdoun

item.title: Input-to-state stability in integral norms for linear infinite-dimensional systems
item.description: arXiv:2501.07680v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study integral-to-integral input-to-state stability for infinite-dimensional linear systems with inputs and trajectories in $L^p$-spaces. We start by developing the corresponding admissibility theory for linear systems with unbounded input operators. While input-to-state stability is typically characterised by exponential stability and finite-time admissibility, we show that this equivalence does not extend directly to integral norms. For analytic semigroups, we establish a precise characterisation using maximal regularity theory. Additionally, we provide direct Lyapunov theorems and construct Lyapunov functions for $L^p$-$L^q$-ISS and demonstrate the results with examples, including diagonal systems and diffusion equations.
item.dc:creator: Sahiba Arora, Andrii Mironchenko

item.title: Modified Polyhedral Method to Elicit Shape-Free Utility and Reduction of Conservatism in Robust Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2503.23269v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we propose a modified polyhedral method to elicit a decision maker's (DM's) nonlinear univariate utility function without explicit knowledge of its shape, Lipschitz modulus, or inflection point. Inspired by \cite{THS04} for linear multivariate utility elicitation, we extend the polyhedral method to the nonlinear setting by addressing two major challenges. First, we approximate the nonlinear utility function using a continuous piecewise linear function (PLF) represented by its increment vector, such that utility elicitation can be viewed as progressively reducing a polyhedral feasible region of increment vectors. Second, we iteratively shrink this polyhedron through hyperplane cuts generated from pairwise lottery comparisons. Since PLF approximation errors may cause the resulting hyperplanes to deviate from ideal cutting directions, we dynamically enrich the PLF by incorporating newly generated lottery outcomes as additional breakpoints. The elicited responses are then used to construct an ambiguity set of utility functions for decision making under worst-case expected utility. To mitigate the potential conservatism of the resulting maximin model, we use the analytic center of the ambiguity set as a nominal estimate of the DM's utility increment vector and derive, through dual reformulation, a flexible weighting scheme for controlling conservatism. The resulting model accommodates asymmetric bounds on utility increments around the analytic center and admits a single mixed-integer linear programming reformulation for piecewise linear utilities. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed elicitation method and conservatism-reduction approach. Finally, we discuss several potential extensions, including applications to multivariate nonlinear utility elicitation and dynamic pricing problems.
item.dc:creator: Sainan Zhang, Shaoyan Guo, Melvyn Sim, Huifu Xu

item.title: Coupled Adaptable Backward-Forward-Backward Resolvent Splitting Algorithm (CABRA): A Matrix-Parametrized Resolvent Splitting Method for the Sum of Maximal Monotone and Cocoercive Operators Composed with Linear Coupling Operators
item.description: arXiv:2505.13927v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a novel matrix-parametrized frugal splitting algorithm which finds a zero of a sum of maximal monotone and cocoercive operators composed with linear selection operators, which models a large class of problems in which the operators take only a subset of decision variables as their input. We also develop a semidefinite programming framework for selecting matrix parameters and demonstrate its use for designing matrix parameters which provide beneficial diagonal scaling, allow parallelization, and adhere to a given communication structure. We show that making use of the structure of the linear selection operators in this way improves convergence in numerical experiments. Even when the selection operators are the identity, we can enhance convergence by using the matrix parameters to provide appropriately chosen diagonal scaling. We conclude by demonstrating the applicability of this algorithm to multi-stage stochastic programming, outlining a decentralized approach to the relaxed stochastic weapon target assignment problem which splits over the source nodes and has low data transfer and memory requirements.
item.dc:creator: Peter Barkley, Robert L. Bassett

item.title: Controllability of finite-dimensional linear fractional systems under uncertain parameters
item.description: arXiv:2508.02420v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates the controllability of finite-dimensional linear fractional systems involving an uncertain parameter. We establish new results on the simultaneous and average controllability. In particular, we show that average controllability can be characterized by the so-called average Kalman rank condition and the average Gramian matrix. Moreover, using the average Gramian matrix, we design an open-loop control with minimal energy. These results can be seen as a natural generalization of the classical results known for systems with integer-order derivatives. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to robustly validate the theoretical findings, with a focus on the fractional R\"ossler system for a damping parameter following either a Gaussian or a uniform distribution.
item.dc:creator: Idriss Boutaayamou, Fouad Et-Tahri, Lahcen Maniar

item.title: Prescribed Performance Control of Uncertain Higher Relative Degree Nonlinear Systems in the Presence of Delays
item.description: arXiv:2509.08601v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a novel feedback controller for a class of uncertain higher relative degree nonlinear systems, subject to delays in both state measurement and control input signals. Building on the prescribed performance control framework, a delay-dependent performance correction mechanism is introduced to ensure the boundedness of all signals in the closed-loop and to keep the output tracking error strictly within a dynamically adjusted performance envelope. This mechanism adapts in response to large delays that may cause performance degradation. In the absence of delays, the correction term vanishes, and the controller recovers the nominal (user-defined) performance envelope. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is validated through simulation studies.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Berger, Lampros N. Bikas, Jan Hachmeister, George A. Rovithakis

item.title: Optimal Diagonal Preconditioning Beyond Worst-Case Conditioning: Theory and Practice of Omega Scaling
item.description: arXiv:2509.23439v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study optimal diagonal preconditioning using the classical worst-case $\kappa$-condition number and the averaging-based $\omega$-condition number. For the $\kappa$-optimal preconditioning problem, we derive an affine-based pseudoconvex reformulation with three key advantages: all stationary points are global minima, subgradients are inexpensive to compute, and the optimization variable is an $n$-dimensional vector rather than an $n\times n$ matrix as in semidefinite programming (SDP) approaches. We develop a simple and highly efficient subgradient method, with convergence guarantees, for solving this pseudoconvex formulation that is substantially more scalable and accurate than existing SDP-based methods. For the $\omega$-condition number, we provide explicit characterizations of optimal diagonal and block diagonal preconditioners. In particular, we show that several classical preconditioners, including Jacobi and row/column normalization, are $\omega$-optimal, and that matrix balancing schemes monotonically reduce $\omega$ and converge to stationary points of the two-sided problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unified and explicit characterization of optimality conditions for both $\kappa$ and $\omega$-based preconditioning. Our numerical experiments further reveal a striking phenomenon: although $\kappa$-optimal preconditioners achieve stronger reductions in the worst-case condition number, $\omega$-optimal preconditioners are substantially cheaper to compute and yield better performance for iterative methods such as preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) and least squares method (LSQR). Moreover, applying $\omega$-optimal scaling to linear systems that are already $\kappa$-optimally preconditioned leads to further improvements in PCG iterations.
item.dc:creator: Saeed Ghadimi, Woosuk L. Jung, Arnesh Sujanani, David Torregrosa-Bel\'en, Henry Wolkowicz

item.title: Distributed Stochastic Proximal Algorithm on Riemannian Submanifolds for Weakly-convex Functions
item.description: arXiv:2510.22270v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper aims to investigate the distributed stochastic optimization problems on compact embedded submanifolds (in the Euclidean space) where the local cost functions are weakly-convex. To address the manifold structure, we propose a distributed Riemannian stochastic proximal algorithm framework by utilizing the retraction and Riemannian consensus protocol, and analyze three specific algorithms: the distributed Riemannian stochastic subgradient, proximal point, and prox-linear algorithms. When the initial points satisfy certain conditions, we show that the iterates generated by this framework converge to a nearly stationary point in expectation while achieving consensus. We further establish the convergence rate of the algorithm framework as $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1+\kappa_g}{\sqrt{k}})$ where $k$ denotes the number of iterations and $\kappa_g$ shows the impact of manifold geometry on the algorithm performance. Finally, numerical experiments are implemented to demonstrate the theoretical results and show the empirical performance.
item.dc:creator: Jishu Zhao, Xi Wang, Jinlong Lei, Shixiang Chen

item.title: On the Convergence of Constrained Gradient Method
item.description: arXiv:2511.17430v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The constrained gradient method (CGM) has recently been proposed to solve convex optimization and monotone variational inequality (VI) problems with general functional constraints. While existing literature has established convergence results for CGM, the assumptions employed therein are quite restrictive; in some cases, certain assumptions are mutually inconsistent, leading to gaps in the underlying analysis. This paper derives rigorous and improved convergence guarantees for CGM under weaker and more reasonable assumptions, covering strongly convex optimization problems, as well as VI problems under both strongly monotone and general monotone settings. Preliminary numerical experiments are provided to verify the validity of CGM and demonstrate its efficacy in addressing such problems.
item.dc:creator: Danqing Zhou, Hongmei Chen, Shiqian Ma, Junfeng Yang

item.title: Sample-Efficient Counterfactual Tuning for Compressor Pressure Control
item.description: arXiv:2512.03747v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In controlled industrial environments, ensuring safety and performance during controller tuning is a challenging and critical task. In particular, control loops in compressor-plenum-throttle systems cannot tolerate costly interruptions, and aggressive excitation may lead to unsafe operating regimes. Given the wide availability of historical data, this paper introduces a counterfactual explainability approach for sample-efficient retuning of compressor control loops. The proposed data-driven algorithm determines, without an explicit plant model or previous control law, the smallest controller adjustment required to achieve predefined performance specifications while guaranteeing stability. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Process Control, Volume 162, pages 103723, 2026
item.dc:creator: Margarita A. Guerrero, Rodrigo A. Gonz\'alez, Cristian R. Rojas

item.title: Time-Invariant Linear Quadratic Regulators: A New Look
item.description: arXiv:2512.10641v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper demonstrates that linear ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients serve as the main building block for time-invariant linear quadratic regulators (LQRs). By applying the Euler-Lagrange equations to a flat output, i.e., to a basis of the free finitely-generated module over the commutative principal ideal ring of time-invariant linear differential operators with respect to the time derivation, this result emerges directly. In module-theoretic terms. The freeness of this structure corresponds to the classical Kalman controllability condition (M. Fliess, Some basic structural properties of generalized linear systems, Syst. Contr. Lett., 15 (1990) 391-396). Within this framework, the two-point boundary value problem, including the control variables, becomes analytically tractable, enabling the derivation of optimal time horizons, optimal parameter design, and rest-to-rest trajectories. Furthermore, a novel turnpike-like phenomenon is established via nonstandard analysis. The feedback loop is closed thanks to the HEOL approach (C. Join, E. Delaleau, M. Fliess, Flatness-based control revisited: The HEOL setting, C.R. Math., 362 (2024) 1693-1706), an extension of model-free control (MFC) that leverages intelligent controllers. Our viewpoint, which significantly simplifies the presentation by avoiding the conventional Kalman state-space representation, relies on foundational algebraic concepts that, while elementary, are rarely used in today's control theory. To aid intuition, some rudimentary examples are presented, most of which include computer simulations.
item.dc:creator: C\'edric Join, Emmanuel Delaleau, Michel Fliess

item.title: On IDA-PBC with Maximum Energy Shapeability
item.description: arXiv:2601.01385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interconnection and Damping Assignment Passivity-Based Control (IDA-PBC) is a well-established stabilization technique for affine nonlinear systems. However, its application is generally hindered by the requirement of solving a set of partial differential equations (PDEs), i.e., the so-called matching equation. This paper explores the notion of maximum energy shapeability which describes the scenario that the homogeneous part of the matching equation admits $m$ independent solutions with $m$ the dimension of the control input. We show that the maximum energy shapeability enables a systematic procedure for the IDA-PBC design by transforming the matching equation into a set of new PDEs. Specifically, the transformed matching equation admits an explicit solution in the single input case. Sufficient conditions for maximum energy shapeability are also provided. It is shown that some existing constructive IDA-PBC designs actually implicitly exploit the maximum energy shapeability. The proposed procedure for the IDA-PBC design is demonstrated with two practical examples.
item.dc:creator: Chengshuai Wu, Wenbin Liu, Meng Zhang, Jianchen Hu, Romeo Ortega

item.title: Adapting Polyhedral Dominance Cones to Ordinal Preference Structures
item.description: arXiv:2601.02796v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In combinatorial optimization, ordinal costs can be used to model the quality of elements whenever numerical values are not available. When considering, for example, routing problems for cyclists, the safety of a street can be ranked in ordered categories like safe (separate bike lane), medium safe (street with a bike lane) and unsafe (street without a bike lane). However, ordinal optimization may suggest unrealistic solutions with huge detours to avoid unsafe street segments. In this paper, we investigate how partial preference information regarding the relative quality of the ordinal categories can be used to improve the relevance of the computed solutions. By introducing preference weights which describe how much better a category is at least or at most, compared to the subsequent category, we enlarge the ordinal dominance cone. This leads to a smaller set of alternatives, i. e., of ordinally efficient solutions. The corresponding weighted ordinal ordering cone is a polyhedral cone and we provide descriptions via its extreme rays and via its facets. The latter implies a linear transformation to an associated multi-objective optimization problem w. r. t. Pareto dominance. This paves the way for the application of standard multi-objective solution approaches. We demonstrate the usefulness of the weighted ordinal ordering cone by investigating a safest path problem with different preference weights. Moreover, we investigate the interrelation between the weighted ordering cone to standard dominance concepts of multi-objective optimization, like, e. g., Pareto dominance, lexicographic dominance and weighted sum dominance.
item.dc:creator: Kathrin Klamroth, Michael Stiglmayr, Julia Sudhoff Santos

item.title: Inverse Stochastic Control via Generalized Schr\"odinger Problems
item.description: arXiv:2601.09210v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a variational formulation of an inverse problem in continuous-time stochastic control, aimed at identifying control costs consistent with a given distribution over trajectories. The formulation is based on minimizing the suboptimality gap of observed behavior. We establish a connection between the inverse problem and a generalized dynamic Schr\"odinger problem, showing that their optimal values coincide. This result links inverse stochastic control with stochastic optimal transport, offering a new conceptual viewpoint on inverse inference in controlled diffusions.
item.dc:creator: Yumiharu Nakano

item.title: Balancing adaptability and predictability: K-revision multistage stochastic programming
item.description: arXiv:2601.12166v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A standard assumption in multistage stochastic programming is that decisions are made after observing the uncertainty from the prior stage. The resulting solutions can be difficult to implement in practice, as they leave practitioners ill-prepared for future stages. To provide better foresight, we introduce the K-revision approach. This new framework requires plans to be specified in advance. To maintain flexibility, we allow plans to be revised a maximum of K times as new information becomes available. We analyze the complexity of K-revision problems, showing NP-hardness even in a simple setting. We examine, both theoretically and computationally, the impact of the K-revision approach on the objective compared with classical multistage stochastic programming models and the partially adaptive approach introduced in [1, 2]. We develop two MIP formulations, one directly from our definition and the other based on a combinatorial characterization. We analyze the tightness of these formulations and propose several methods to strengthen them. Computational experiments on synthetic problems and practical applications demonstrate that our approach is both computationally tractable and effective in reaching near-optimal performance while increasing the predictability of the solutions produced.
item.dc:creator: Chengwenjian Wang, Alexander S. Estes, Jean-Philippe P. Richard

item.title: Tight semidefinite programming relaxations for sparse box-constrained quadratic programs
item.description: arXiv:2601.18545v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a new class of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations for sparse box-constrained quadratic programs, obtained by a novel integration of the Reformulation Linearization Technique into standard SDP relaxations while explicitly exploiting the sparsity of the problem. The resulting relaxations are not implied by some of the most widely-used LP and SDP relaxations for this class of optimization problems. We establish a sufficient condition under which the convex hull of the feasible region of the lifted quadratic program is SDP-representable; the proof is constructive and yields an explicit extended formulation. Although the resulting SDP may be of exponential size in general, we further identify additional structural conditions on the sparsity of the optimization problem that guarantee the existence of a polynomial-size SDP-representable formulation, which can be constructed in polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Aida Khajavirad

item.title: From Consensus-Based Optimization to Evolution Strategies: Proof of Global Convergence
item.description: arXiv:2602.11677v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Consensus-based optimization (CBO) is a powerful and versatile zero-order multi-particle method designed to provably solve high-dimensional global optimization problems, including those that are genuinely nonconvex or nonsmooth. The method relies on a balance between stochastic exploration and contraction toward a consensus point, which is defined via the Laplace principle as a proxy for the global minimizer. In this paper, we introduce new CBO variants that address practical and theoretical limitations of the original formulation of this novel optimization methodology. First, we propose a model called $\delta$-CBO}, which incorporates nonvanishing diffusion to prevent premature collapse to suboptimal states. We also develop a numerically stable implementation, the Consensus Freezing scheme, that remains robust even for arbitrarily large time steps by freezing the consensus point over time intervals. We connect these models through appropriate asymptotic limits. Furthermore, we derive from the Consensus Freezing scheme by suitable time rescaling and asymptotics a further algorithm, the Consensus Hopping scheme, which can be interpreted as a form of $(1,\lambda)$-Evolution Strategy. For all these schemes, we characterize for the first time the invariant measures and establish global convergence results, including exponential convergence rates.
item.dc:creator: Massimo Fornasier, Hui Huang, Jona Klemenc, Greta Malaspina

item.title: Lyapunov characterization of boundedness of reachability sets for infinite-dimensional systems
item.description: arXiv:2603.04190v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove a converse Lyapunov theorem for boundedness of reachability sets for a general class of control systems whose flow is Lipschitz continuous on compact intervals with respect to trajectory-dominated inputs. We show that this condition is satisfied by broad classes of semilinear evolution equations. For ordinary differential equations, as a consequence of our results, we obtain a converse Lyapunov theorem for forward completeness, without a priori restrictions on the magnitude of inputs. As an example, we rederive Wintner's classical result using our Lyapunov approach.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Bachmann, Andrii Mironchenko

item.title: The Popov's Algorithm with Optimal Bounded Stepsize for Generalized Monotone Variational Inequalities
item.description: arXiv:2603.06442v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For solving unconstrained generalized monotone variational inequality, we prove that the iterations generated by Popov algorithm converge to a solution when stepsize is smaller than $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}L}$, where $L$ is the Lipschitz constant of the variational inequality operator. The convergence analysis is carried out by using a new Lyapunov-type function. In addition, we prove that the upper bound $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}L}$ is tight. Finally, we extend the results to variational inequality with linear subspace constraints.
item.dc:creator: Nhung Hong Nguyen, Thanh Quoc Trinh, Phan Tu Vuong

item.title: Long-Run Conditional Value at Risk Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2603.09734v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a reinforcement learning method for minimizing the long-run conditional value at risk (CVaR) in Markov decision processes with finite state and action spaces. The method uses a single sample trajectory to update a quantile estimate, a $Q$-function, and a randomized policy, without requiring knowledge of transition probabilities or cost distributions. Under appropriate conditions, we show that the estimates track their changing targets as the policy is updated and exploration decreases, even when the proportion of updates for some state and action pairs tends to zero. With a strict action gap, the policy converges to a locally optimal deterministic policy if it enters a suitable neighborhood sufficiently late. We also extend the method to an objective combining CVaR and mean cost. Numerical experiments illustrate its performance in machine replacement and energy storage and compare it with existing methods.
